\chapter{Synthesis --- Supposing Out Loud}
\label{ch:sintesis-condiciones}
\hlchaptermodality{210}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can speak about a world that does not exist.}

I can speak about a world that does not exist.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — supposing out loud}

\label{lesson:ES-C56-sintesis-condiciones}



\begin{quote}
Build the supposing form of \emph{ser}. (\emph{Fuera}.) Of \emph{hacer}. (\emph{Hiciera}.)

Now use one.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Say these, and hear how much each one carries:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Si fuera profesor, hablaría español todos los días.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Si tuviera tiempo, comería en casa.}
\end{quote}

Each says what would happen \textbf{and} that it is not happening, in one breath and with no extra words. English needs \emph{but I'm not} to be quite that clear; Spanish puts it in the verb endings.

\textbf{This is the first thing in this book you can say about a world that does not exist.} Everything before it described what is, was, or will be.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the climb cost}]
Look back at what this one sentence needed.

It needed \emph{si}, which cost one chapter. It needed the \emph{-ría} form, which you had already. And it needed the supposing form — which needed the \textbf{preterite plural}, a gap nobody would have named as the thing standing between you and hypothetical speech.

That is worth remembering the next time something in this language looks arbitrary. The order things must be learned in is rarely the order they look important in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Si fuera profesor, hablaría español todos los días}
  \item an unreal condition of your own
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What can you now say that you could not before? (Something about a world that \textbf{is not the case}.) And what had to be built first? (The \textbf{preterite plural} — and nobody would have guessed it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[depende]{depende — the condition you do not have to finish}

\label{lesson:ES-C56-depende}



\begin{quote}
You have spent two chapters building conditions with both halves: \emph{si} plus a situation, then what follows. This is the word for when you want the condition without saying what it is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item supposing out loud — the real and unreal conditions this word stands in for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Three syllables, stress in the middle: \emph{de-PEN-de}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{depende} — \textquotedblleft{}it depends.\textquotedblright{} Latin \emph{de-} (\textquotedblleft{}down from\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{pendere} (\textquotedblleft{}to hang\textquotedblright{}). To depend on something is to \textbf{hang from} it, and the metaphor is still doing work: the answer is suspended from a condition, and until the condition settles the answer swings.

That \emph{pendere} is a generous root. It gave English \textbf{pendant} (a thing that hangs), \textbf{pending} (still hanging), \textbf{suspend}, and — by way of a hanging scale pan — \textbf{pensive} and even \textbf{pound}, because things were weighed by hanging them.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every condition you have built so far names its own \emph{si}. \emph{Depende} is the one that does not: it asserts that a condition exists and declines to state it, which is why it is such a useful answer to a question you are not ready to answer.

Add \emph{de} and you can name it after all — \emph{depende de ti}, \textquotedblleft{}it depends on you.\textquotedblright{} The condition stops being a mystery and becomes a thing you point at.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{depende} — stress the middle
  \item name the condition — \emph{depende de ti}
  \item the same answer the long way, with a full \emph{si} sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{pendere} mean, and what is hanging? (To hang — the answer hangs from the condition.) Which English words share the root? (\textbf{Pendant}, \textbf{pending}, \textbf{suspend}.) What do you add to name the condition? (\emph{De}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
